bottom_line.paragraph: The asking price of $474,900 sits in the upper part of what recent sales support. It isn't out of line, but it isn't a bargain either. The two sales that support this price closed in the spring, when mortgage rates were lower and homes were selling faster. The recent sales and this home's own history point lower.

history.heading: This home has been for sale since January
history.intro: The current listing shows 36 days on the market. That number only counts the second listing. The full history:
rows: Taken off the market twice, put back each time
Contract fell apart; taken off the market
Back on market at a higher price
Relisted as a new listing, which reset the day count
history.after: That adds up to about 119 days of active marketing across two listings, spread over eight months, plus one failed contract. The market has had a long look at this home in the $475,000–$485,000 range, and no buyer has closed. That doesn't mean something is wrong with the house, but we need to know why the April contract fell apart before writing an offer.

offer_plan.intro: Our recommendation for your offer, based on the comparable sales, the market, and this home's history. These three numbers are a negotiating plan, not a value opinion, so we'll adjust them together if anything changes.
offer_plan.why_opening: The bottom of the supported range, backed by the comps. After eight months, four price cuts, and a failed contract, the seller has reason to negotiate rather than ignore it.
offer_plan.why_target: Where recent sales and the typical 3.5% negotiation suggest this home settles.
offer_plan.why_walk_away: About the median of the adjusted comps. Above it you'd be paying spring-market prices and risking a low appraisal you'd have to cover in cash.
offer_plan.conditions: the roof is documented as new, the April contract fell through for reasons unrelated to the house, and no other offers are competing. If any of those changes, we'll revisit the numbers before you sign.

offer.heading: Negotiating Points
bullets: There is room to negotiate. The seller is paying to carry a vacant house, has cut the price four times, and has already lost one buyer. Mortgage rates are also higher now than when the spring sales happened.

Seller help with closing costs is normal right now. Eight of the last ten sales in this area included seller-paid costs, typically around $10,000. Asking for a credit instead of a lower price can reduce the cash you need at closing.

Watch the appraisal. Only two homes in Spring Oaks have sold above this home's price per square foot, both renovated pool homes. An offer above about $480,000 raises the chance the appraisal comes in low, which you would have to cover in cash or renegotiate.

comps.intro: We looked at every sale within one mile since April 2026 and chose the five closest matches: Spring Oaks pool homes of about 1,800–1,900 square feet, built in the 1970s. We included the ones that argue against a lower price. For each sale, we adjust for differences so it reflects what that home would have sold for if it were this one.
comps.method_note: Adjustments used: about $75 per square foot of size difference; $30,000–$45,000 for a home that hadn't been renovated to this level; $5,000–$10,000 for a noticeably larger or better lot; 1–2% off spring sales because prices have softened since. Seller-paid costs are subtracted from the sale price, since they reduce what the seller actually received. Condition adjustments are based on listing descriptions, not visits, so they are judgment calls.

comps.summary_paragraph: The adjusted values run from about $436,000 to $492,000, with a median of $469,800. We lean toward the middle because the two highest sales are the best condition matches but come from a stronger market, while the lowest two needed the biggest adjustments. Other Spring Oaks sales support the same picture: 607 Green Briar Blvd (a 2014 renovation, pool) sold for $427,000 in April, and 623 Lakespur Ln (renovated, no pool) sold for $435,000 in May.

scatter.heading: The Whole Neighborhood at a Glance
scatter.intro: Every sale within one mile since April and every home for sale now, plotted by size and price. The dashed line is the trend for all sales based on size alone. At 1,849 square feet, it sits around {trend_at_subject}.
scatter.after_paragraph: The trend line isn't a value estimate for this house. It lumps dated homes and homes without pools together with renovated ones, and size explains {r2_share} of the difference in sale prices here. What the chart shows is where this home sits: renovated pool homes sell well above the line, and 517 Hickorywood is asking right among them, near the top of the shaded range the adjustments support. Only two Spring Oaks sales of similar size closed higher. Meanwhile, 644 Peachwood, a renovated home of the same size without a pool, is for sale well below.

market.intro: We looked at 35 sales within one mile of this home between April and mid-September 2026. The market has cooled noticeably since spring.
rows: Typical Sale vs. Original Asking Price
Typical Days to Go Under Contract
bullets: Homes are selling for about 3.5% under their original asking price, compared with full price in the spring. Sellers are now expecting to negotiate.

Inventory is balanced. There are 15 homes for sale in this area, and at the summer pace of sales that's about four months of supply. That's neither a buyer's market nor a seller's market, but it has shifted toward buyers. Six in ten current listings have already cut their price.

Mortgage rates are up. The national average 30-year rate was 6.95% the week of September 17, versus roughly 6.2–6.4% during the spring sales. That's the main reason the spring prices are harder to repeat now.

Price per square foot. Spring Oaks homes have sold for a median of about $231 per square foot since April. This home is asking $257. That's supportable for a renovated pool home, but only two Spring Oaks sales have been higher.

taxes.heading: Property taxes will be much higher than the listing shows
taxes.intro: The listing shows $2,731 in taxes. That's the 2024 bill, based on a previous owner's assessment. In Florida, a home's taxable value is reset when it sells, so your bill will be based on roughly what you pay. You also get to file for your own homestead exemption.
taxes.note: Based on 2025 final millage rates (13.6790 unincorporated; 17.5683 City of Altamonte Springs). We still need to confirm which applies; the property appraiser's record shows it. These estimates assume the county values the home at the purchase price, and it often values homes somewhat lower, so treat these as the high end. Garbage and other flat assessments aren't included. File for homestead by March 1 of the year after you close.
taxes.after_paragraph: Your first year matters. Your lender will likely set up your escrow using the seller's lower bill. When your own higher bill arrives, your monthly payment can rise to cover the difference. Budget for the higher number from the start.

insurance.paragraph: The main things that drive the cost for this house are the roof's age, the 1972 construction (especially the wiring and plumbing), wind-mitigation features, and the pool. The flood zone (X) means flood insurance isn't required, though it's inexpensive and still worth considering. Get a real quote during your inspection period, after the 4-point and wind-mitigation inspections. The payment estimates below use $3,600 a year as a placeholder, not a quote.

payment.intro: Three common ways to finance this home at the full asking price. Your lender will give you exact numbers.

credit_scenarios.intro: The seller cares about what they net; you may care more about the cash you need at closing. These three offers leave the seller with about the same amount but split it differently between price and a credit toward your closing costs.
credit_scenarios.after_paragraph: Each $5,000 of credit saves you about $4,600 at closing and costs about $41 a month. That's worth it if cash is tight or you might sell within a decade, and less so if you have savings to spare and plan to stay long term. All three prices sit below the median adjusted comp, so the appraisal should support any of them.

items: The roof. The first version of this listing described a brand-new roof. The current listing doesn't mention the roof at all. Roof age is the biggest factor in insuring a Florida home, so we want the permit and date in writing.
Why the April contract fell apart. If a previous buyer walked away over an inspection or appraisal problem, we want to know what it was.

Wiring and plumbing from 1972. Homes of this age in Spring Oaks often have aluminum branch wiring and original cast-iron drains. Insurers ask about both. Add a sewer-line camera inspection to the general inspection.
Permits for the renovation. Confirm the kitchen, bath, and any electrical or plumbing work was permitted. Unpermitted work can cause problems with insurance and future resale.
The fourth bedroom. Check that the property appraiser's record shows four bedrooms, and if a room was converted, confirm it was permitted.
AC age and pool equipment. Neither is listed. Also confirm the pool has a compliant safety barrier.
"As-Is" doesn't mean no inspection. The As-Is contract still gives you an inspection period in which you can cancel for any reason. It only means the seller isn't committing to repairs.
questions: When was the roof replaced? Can you share the permit and a copy of the roof, 4-point, or wind-mitigation report?
Why did the April contract fall apart, and were there inspection or appraisal reports from that buyer?
How old are the AC and the pool equipment? Does the home have aluminum branch wiring, and what brand is the electrical panel?
Were the kitchen, bathroom, and any electrical or plumbing updates permitted?
Is the fourth bedroom original to the house?
Is the seller open to contributing toward the buyer's closing costs?

method: This analysis uses the Stellar MLS listing and full price history for 517 Hickorywood Ave, a Stellar MLS search of single-family homes within one mile (sales from April 6 to September 17, 2026, plus current active, pending, and expired listings), Seminole County Property Appraiser 2025 final millage rates, and the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage rate survey for September 17, 2026.

This is a broker's opinion of value based on comparable sales. It is not an appraisal. A lender's appraiser works under different standards and may reach a different number. Tax, insurance, and payment figures are estimates for planning, not quotes, so confirm them with your lender and insurance agent. Market conditions change, so this analysis should be refreshed if you haven't made an offer within a few weeks.
